how: Starters propose familiar figures or report work already begun while asking others to finish and maintain it.
Repeated calls recruit builders for repair and redirect scarce participants toward the existing threatened work.
Familiar figures become candidate marks whose scale, additions, and relation to existing work remain open to discussion.
Members report placement and remaining work through short completion answers and instructions about unfinished parts.
Anchor coordinates, revised tile locations, pixel counts, and a gridded reference make shared construction actionable.
Defenders repeatedly repair overwrites, rally against incoming expansion, and concentrate limited effort on the figure's face.
A restorer identifies their own mistaken repair and offers to join the relocation after learning what the builders intended.
Members enforce restraint through consultation rules, protection of negotiated boundaries, promises to restore neighboring work, and warnings against destruction.
An overlap dispute becomes an accepted bargain exchanging space to finish one image for help moving the neighboring image.
Members consider invading a neighboring flag and encounter its greater dedication, instantiating an attack proposal without demonstrating execution.
Pressure on the existing site prompts relocation proposals, moves, smaller designs, and continuing disagreement about whether to hold ground.
Members celebrate intermediate completion, credit their own placing, and thank collaborators before the original canvas's final outcome is known.
After closure, members mourn destroyed community art, name its missing final presence, and seek a timelapse of repeated destruction.
Members carry the work onto replacement canvases through renewed calls, claimed space, reported completion, and further additions.
A local request for an automatic placement script does not establish adoption, while the reported running mini-flag script belongs to the visiting opponent.
A coordinate instruction receives the bare completion answer Placed it without a request for anything in return.
Requests for help receive offers of reciprocal protection, redirection toward the existing build, or limits on what spare help can do.
A Discord invitation connects joint building to an alliance that participants later celebrate and describe as mutual repair.
The contest continues after closure through complaints about forced movement, an opponent's admitted intent, and judgments that small community art had little chance.
Seeking host space requires asking about negotiation, submitting an application, and checking permission before starting another image.
A suggestion to concentrate defence in an original thread does not establish host moderation, a canvas posting rule, or a dispute over the canvas flood.
A missed compromise message and a request to stop an opponent's script do not establish an explicit dispute about who may bind a room.
Post-event speakers contest responsibility by defending a negotiated neighbor relationship against an opponent's account of the loss.
Members anticipate channel pranks, archive earlier ones, test a fake episode, and acknowledge being fooled alongside their canvas work.
Members judge the canvas crowded and the desired work difficult to fit while debating smaller versions and the limits of current defence.
The concept naming the opponent explains relocation through its current deletion of the artwork rather than identifying an inherited quarrel.
Familiar jokes and characters provide the proposed marks, including tiny versions that retain their shared meaning at a single pixel.
Local declarations and negotiations show practical organization but cannot test a numerical claim about how most rooms organized or establish appointed authority here.
Familiar references supply desired artwork, but the coded rival and invasion turns do not identify a prior tie as their reason for attacking.
Members contact a neighboring moderator, propose a compromise, and report its terms back to their room without a demonstrated formal appointment.
A coordinate instruction is answered by a direct report of placement, supporting recruitment into a specific task rather than estimating silent participation.
Reporting an already started figure and asking others to finish it occur in the same turn, giving helpers a concrete project to join.
A report of completed repairs and renewed expansion receives a report that the attack resumed, returning the existing work to maintenance.
Keeping the work includes asking a neighboring moderator not to overwrite it and asking visiting builders to change their overlap.
Members explicitly recall the skull compromise and make staying away from that boundary a defence rule that preserves the alliance effort.
Defence prompts an automation request, but local adoption remains unobserved and the reported running script belongs to a visiting opponent.
A replacement-canvas completion report also celebrates collective success, joining achievement and marking it within a single turn.
Celebration and a later request for a destruction timelapse are documented, but the concepts do not establish celebration as the request's cause.
Loss recording precedes successor-canvas building, but the concepts do not establish a preserved image or account as the reason either platform was chosen.
Judging a site untenable does not itself end defence because continued fighting is explicitly required until an organized rebuilding destination exists.
Published references and coordinates remain revisable while builders dispute scale, wing timing, and how construction should signal a boundary to neighbors.
A bare completion answer occurs, but other acceptances depend on the project proceeding or spare time between defence, and silent placers remain unobservable.
A request for outside help is answered with difficulty defending the existing work and then an offer to exchange protection for help.
The boundary proposal itself exchanges construction help for space and receives explicit acceptance rather than merely preceding later cooperation.
Attack consideration and a withdrawn sleeping-hours proposal are documented without establishing that recruitment caused either proposal or an executed offensive.
The sleeping-hours proposal is withdrawn in favor of cooperation, and a repair call receives an explicit instruction against degrading the opponent's work.
A visiting neighbor's war claim receives a direct compromise proposal, which the visitor accepts as a trade of space and help.
Later contest talk responds to incoming expansion and the visitor's admitted intent, without demonstrating that an outgoing attack by the focal room produced the rivalry.
The alliance is negotiated through an overlap settlement, while common-threat causation remains unestablished despite participants later crediting the alliance with sustaining defence.
Calls and voluntary defence-thread consolidation do not establish that a canvas flood caused a host governance response.
The accepted compromise and later missed-message diagnosis do not establish negotiation causing a dispute over who may commit the room.
Diagnosis first checks whether an apparent contribution occurred on the real shared canvas rather than a free-draw client.
Explaining a mistaken restoration is followed by an apology, an offer to help the move, and acceptance of the apology.
Joint coordination relays invitations into chat and brings the compromise and a reference back into the public thread without revealing the full chat process.
Additional reciprocal help is limited by current defence demands and the obligation to preserve existing multi-room compromises.
Recognizing a host's approval and submitting an application establish attempted entry but do not establish acceptance or actual occupation under the host's rule.
Finding an image or posting a terse recognition title cannot alone establish that the focal room made, owned, completed, or collectively celebrated it.
The ambivalent missing-Fred title precedes closure and therefore cannot be treated as retrospective evidence about the final canvas's outcome.
Members preserve an earlier prank by recovering lost material, identifying an omission, and checking what the missing item contained.
Successor-canvas work returns to recruitment when a report of another disappearance receives a direct proposal to make another image.
Recognizing a mistaken restoration recruits its author as a helper for the relocation rather than simply removing an obstacle.
The same edited post moves directly from celebrating completion to proposing the next figure, reopening design after an intermediate success.
An original-canvas relocation call receives a new anchor coordinate and then a placement report, explicitly returning a move to building.
A separate Wikipedia prank recruits a familiar figure, receives a correction of its claimed permission, and is subsequently reverted.
Post-event thanks carry a valued neighbor relationship into an expressed preference for the next canvas event.
